sections.heading: Call Cadence Change to Monthly
sections.summary: No objections to moving calls from bi-weekly to monthly, given async progress on Telegram and Justin's Hegota workload.
sections.body:
- Justin proposed switching from bi-weekly to monthly calls, citing his new role as Besu lead for Hegota and the risk of inconsistent scheduling.
- Alternative offered: keep bi-weekly but have someone else run every other call.
- The group is still in the design phase, with substantial async communication happening on Telegram.
- No objections raised; monthly cadence adopted.

sections.heading: Post-Quantum Threshold Encryption Status
sections.summary: PQ threshold decryption remains off the table until cryptographic primitives mature, likely years away.
sections.body:
- Justin proposed formally setting aside PQ threshold encryption, noting the crypto is not mature enough, especially for secret sharing.
- Gottfried clarified the core need is threshold *decryption*, a fundamentally different primitive from threshold signing.
- Benedict (absent) has had some recent ideas (related to the "silent one-shot" paper), but even an inefficient construction with silent setup does not yet exist.
  - Even a conceptually sound but inefficient silent-setup PQ scheme has not been achieved.
- Gottfried estimated the crypto probably won't be ready for years.
- Agreement: park PQ threshold encryption; Justin will continue monitoring PQ signature work (SPHINCS, hash-based signatures) for Hegota.
- Lucid remains the active design since it is already post-quantum secure, with the optionality problem as the main open issue.

sections.heading: Key-Reveal Allowlist: Voting Mechanism Overview
sections.summary: Jannik presented a validator-voted allowlist for key publishers, implemented via an EL voting contract with delegation and incremental tallying.
sections.body:
- The allowlist proposal lets the validator set vote to approve key publisher addresses deemed trustworthy for revealing decryption keys.
- Jannik walked through the design from [the HackMD document](https://hackmd.io/65f2AsqPSSGl4ea_eG2-jQ):
  - Each address is voted on individually; accepted when it reaches 50% of total effective balance support.
  - Design requirements: efficiency, delegation support, responsiveness, and representativeness.
- Delegation is important because most validators (especially home stakers) won't curate the list themselves; they can delegate to entities that monitor key publisher behavior.
- Implementation is proposed as an EL voting contract rather than CL logic, for several reasons:
  - Transaction fees provide built-in spam protection.
  - Easier to specify in Solidity than via new networking/consensus messages.
  - Decoupled from attestation/proposal schedules, enabling faster responsiveness.
  - Downside: validators must send EL transactions to vote.
- The contract manages two things:
  - Ballot lists (permissionless creation/editing of sets of approved addresses by delegates).
  - Validator subscription statements (a validator declares which list they follow).
- Tallying is designed to be incremental — processing contract events one by one rather than recalculating from scratch each block.
  - The main efficiency concern is refreshing vote weights when effective balances change, which requires a full pass over validators.
- Gottfried suggested subsampling a random weighted subset of validators per epoch to reduce tallying cost; Jannik noted this could work but needs benchmarking.
- Key publishers may be required to deposit ETH before being added to a list, to prevent spam from inflating the address set.

sections.heading: Effective Balance Weighting for Votes
sections.summary: Votes must be weighted by effective balance to avoid incentivizing stake splitting; 50% threshold kept as a natural Schelling point.
sections.body:
- Justin questioned whether effective balance should determine voting weight, since stake size doesn't obviously correlate with interest in correct key reveals.
- Gottfried and Anders (in chat) explained the mechanism design rationale: without balance weighting, consolidation is penalized and stake splitting is incentivized.
- 50% of total effective balance was discussed as the acceptance threshold.
  - Gottfried noted 50% is arbitrary but serves as a natural, unopinionated Schelling point.
  - No design constraint enforces exactly 50%; it could be made dynamic.
- Jannik suggested the threshold should be higher than the largest single staker's share to prevent a centralized entity from unilaterally approving a key publisher.
- Jannik also proposed letting the validator set vote on the threshold itself, analogous to gas limit voting.
- On upvotes vs. downvotes: negative voting was discussed but deemed not worth the added complexity.
  - Gottfried floated counting negative votes double but no consensus formed.
  - Agreement to keep voting simple — presence of a vote is endorsement, absence is abstention; validators can vote for an empty list to explicitly abstain.
- Gottfried raised the risk that if voting participation is low and the threshold is based on total validator balance, no key publishers would be approved, making Lucid unusable at launch.

sections.heading: Voting Costs, Spam, and Incentives
sections.summary: Voting transaction costs are paid by validators; key publishers could sponsor votes via paymaster contracts, but no reward mechanism was agreed upon.
sections.body:
- Since voting is implemented as EL transactions, validators pay gas fees to vote.
- Making voting free would create exploitable free block space; rewarding voters introduces complexity around how much and how often to pay.
- Gottfried suggested recording the block at which each validator last voted, as a rate-limiting mechanism against spam.
- Key publishers (as financially incentivized entities) could sponsor voting costs:
  - Via paymaster/bribery contracts that reimburse validators who voted for their list.
  - Could be done trustlessly on-chain without frame transactions.
- No formal incentive or reimbursement mechanism was decided; the default position is validators bear voting costs as a network duty.

sections.heading: Consensus-Specs CL Draft PR: Merge Now or Hold (chat only)
sections.summary: Raised in chat, not on the call: jtraglia wants to merge the CL draft spec, but the one open question is whether key publishers should be in-protocol — exactly what the allowlist discussion is deciding.
sections.body:
- Boma shared [consensus-specs PR #5403](https://github.com/ethereum/consensus-specs/pull/5403#issuecomment-5623731714) in chat, noting jtraglia wants to merge the CL draft and that the only open question is whether key publishers should be in-protocol — the same question the validator allowlist voting discussion is trying to answer.
- The choice framed in chat: merge the current off-protocol base now and update it once the allowlist design settles, or hold the merge until that decision is made.
- Justin replied "i think we should hold it"; Boma acknowledged. No other participant weighed in, and the topic was not discussed aloud on the call.
- Boma asked participants to leave a comment on the PR rather than settle it in chat.

sections.heading: Two-Tier Top-of-Block Ordering as Alternative to Hard Enforcement
sections.summary: Instead of rejecting transactions with non-allowlisted key publishers, prioritize allowlisted ones at top of block while still permitting self-reveal below.
sections.body:
- Anders (in chat) proposed that transactions using allowlisted key publishers be sorted by fee at the top of the block, with non-allowlisted ones sorted by fee below them.
- This replaces the hard enforcement model (where blocks containing non-allowlisted key reveals are invalid) with a softer incentive mechanism.
- Gottfried expressed enthusiasm for the two-tier approach, noting several advantages:
  - Reduces market entry barriers: new key publishers can earn revenue and build a track record before reaching 50% approval, rather than making zero revenue until crossing the threshold.
  - Mitigates competitive manipulation: a competitor bribing validators to push an incumbent below 50% would only demote them to the lower tier rather than eliminating their revenue entirely.
  - Preserves self-reveal capability.
  - Compared favorably to the original Shutter trust-graph design, which was overly restrictive and prescribed too much block ordering; this approach uses just one bit (allowlisted or not).
- Jannik noted the trust graph only diluted optionality but didn't mitigate it, which drew criticism.
- The two-tier model was seen as an incremental improvement that still drives adoption toward allowlisted providers.
- Agreement: the group is excited about this idea and wants to pursue it further.

sections.heading: Lucid EIP Updates and Allowlist Integration
sections.summary: The allowlist will be developed within the existing Lucid EIP (EIP-8184) for now; Jannik invited to open a PR and join as co-author.
sections.body:
- Discussion on whether the allowlist mechanism warrants a separate EIP or should be folded into the existing Lucid EIP (EIP-8184).
  - Gottfried noted the EIP is already large and splitting EL (voting contract) from CL parts might help, but acknowledged you can't ship one without the other.
  - Anders and Jannik expressed no strong preference.
- Decision: keep it as one document for now; can be split later if it becomes unwieldy.
- Jannik encouraged to open a PR into EIP-8184 with the allowlist design; to be added as an author.
- Jannik acknowledged the proposal needs more work before it's EIP-ready.
- Gottfried raised two reminders for EIP updates:
  - One of the hashes in the Lucid EIP needs randomness added — a commitment needs to be hiding.
  - The current 128-fold penalty for non-reveal could potentially be lowered if the allowlist provides an alternative anti-abuse mechanism, improving usability and reducing upfront capital requirements for users.
- Anders noted the Lucid EIP already describes how key publishers can front the penalty on behalf of senders, particularly in the bundle design.
- Batching/bundles: the current EIP includes bundles where fees are amortized, but bundles add significant complexity and may be removed.
- Next steps: async work on Telegram, watch for PRs into EIP-8184, reconvene in one month.
